rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section opens by warning readers not to mistake divine respite as indifference; God's mercy coexists with his power to punish.
rows.anchor: no one should be misconceived by the respite given to him by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prelude characterizes God as gracious and merciful as well as powerful and vengeful.
rows.anchor: He is very gracious and merciful as well as powerful and revengeful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant Quraysh, who demanded that the Prophet show them angels, are warned not to treat the matter lightly.
rows.anchor: who were demanding from the Prophet (sws) to show them angels – are warned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Lot account is historical evidence for the Quraysh, who passed the settlement; those wishing to see angels should prepare for the same fate.
rows.anchor: if they desire to see angels, then they should also get ready to meet the fate of the people of Lot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Respite for both good and evil people does not mean that God regards them as equal.
rows.anchor: one should not take this to mean that both are equal in His eyes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who follow God's straight path face hardships that test their patience, but they ultimately succeed.
rows.anchor: made to pass through various hardships to test their patience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deviate may be granted respite so that the truth is conclusively conveyed to them before their eventual punishment.
rows.anchor: those who deviate from His path may be give some respite so that the truth is conclusively conveyed to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deviate from God's path are ultimately punished for their deviation.
rows.anchor: they are punished for this deviation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels who announced a knowledgeable son to Abraham were the same ones who brought the punishment to Lot's people, substantiating the preceding warning historically.
rows.anchor: glad tidings of a son endowed with knowledge brought the thunder of punishment to the people of Lot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham knew that angels appearing openly had a mission, which made him afraid.
rows.anchor: when angels come openly in this way, they have some mission at hand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Lot's nearby people had reached extreme moral deprivation, Abraham suspected they might be the angels' target.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) could have felt that perhaps they must be the target.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised son would be a prophet, making the glad tidings especially great because prophethood was Abraham's greatest wish for him.
rows.anchor: The greatest desire Abraham (sws) could have had for his son would be that he be a prophet of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham was pleased but, because his old age made the prophecy seem improbable, sought further assurance that the glad tidings came from God.
rows.anchor: he wanted to have further assurance in this regard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ḥaqq here means a certain event.
rows.anchor: here means “a certain event.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels reassured Abraham that God's promise was independent of apparent circumstances because God has power over everything.
rows.anchor: anything which is from God is not dependent on circumstances in any way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once convinced the glad tidings came from God, Abraham spoke spontaneously, expressing gratitude.
rows.anchor: he uttered these words spontaneously. They reflect the gratitude that he felt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's question did not express hopelessness; it arose only because the apparent circumstances conflicted with the glad tidings.
rows.anchor: the question he had posed to the angels was not because he had no hope in God’s mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who despair of God's mercy in the hardest circumstances are deprived of faith and go astray.
rows.anchor: those who lose hope in God’s mercy in the hardest of circumstances are deprived of faith and go astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word khutb is generally used for an important matter.
rows.anchor: mostly used for some important matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having settled his own concern, Abraham reasoned that a group of angels would not come merely to give glad tidings and must have an important task.
rows.anchor: why did the angels come in the form of a group to merely give glad tidings; they must have some important task at hand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham suspected the angels had come for Lot's nation because it lived nearby and its moral degradation had crossed all limits.
rows.anchor: For this reason, he could have thought that perhaps the angels had come for Lot’s nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' choice to call Lot's people wrongdoers rather than name them conveys anger and disdain.
rows.anchor: they did not name their

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Decisive divine punishment comes only when evil has spread to everyone, with no pious people remaining or any survivors living miserably.
rows.anchor: decisive punishment of God visits a nation only when evil spreads

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for Lot's family can include followers, so people beyond his household may also have accepted faith.
rows.anchor: also includes followers, it may well be that some people besides

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels specified the exception before Abraham to allay his fears about Lot's family and followers.
rows.anchor: before Abraham (sws) to allay his fears about Lot’s family and followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's wife's exclusion shows God's law is impartial: even a prophet's wife must face its consequences.
rows.anchor: God’s law is totally unbiased. Even a prophet’s wife must face its consequences.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person close to a prophet who adheres to evil incurs greater divine anger and deserves harsher accountability.
rows.anchor: if a person close to a prophet – whether man or woman – adheres to evil, God is angrier on him than others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot recognized that the visitors were not from his land and expressed surprise, wanting them to identify themselves.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) knew that the angels did not belong to his land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ḥaqq means a certain punishment, as it does in verse 8.
rows.anchor: in the same sense as in verse 8: a certain punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After this declaration, the angels did not need to clarify that they were not human beings.
rows.anchor: it was not necessary for the angels to clarify that they were not human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' assertion that they were absolutely truthful was intended as an admonition to the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: The words “we are absolutely truthful” are meant to admonish the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was told to leave at night with his family for the directed place because torment would visit the city.
rows.anchor: The reason, as is referred to later, is that this place would be visited by a torment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was to walk behind his family like a shepherd behind his herd so none strayed and was eaten by a wolf.
rows.anchor: This is like a shepherd walking behind his herd lest any sheep is separated from it and is consumed by a wolf.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Looking back at a place one has left signals attachment and fondness for it.
rows.anchor: it shows his attachment and fondness to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though ordinary attachment is natural, believers leaving a city condemned after decisive proof should depart with no fondness for it.
rows.anchor: should be done in such a manner by the believers that no fondness remains in their hearts for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition after qadaynā implies an omitted word meaning balaghna, ‘We informed him.’
rows.anchor: shows that a word of the meaning of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city refers to Sodom.
rows.anchor: The city here refers to Soddom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot appealed in humiliation for the people to protect his guests and fear God; such an appeal can work where moral sensitivity remains, since hospitality is honored even among the vile, but has no effect on the insensitive.
rows.anchor: respect for guests is considered to be a noble virtue even among the vilest of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people invented a pretext for their mischief, claiming Lot had outside connections who visited and plotted against them, and fearing a future calamity from him.
rows.anchor: told Lot (sws) that he has connections with people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's offer of his daughters was not a literal offer; it was a final attempt to jolt his people's conscience, as explained under Hūd 78.
rows.anchor: It was a last-ditch effort by him to shake and jolt the conscience of his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some narratives say the Prophet would hurry past settlements destroyed by God's punishment and tell his followers to do likewise.
